Using the product rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))=f(x){g}^{′}(x)+{f}^{′}(x)g(x).
$$

At the point where $x=2$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))|}_{x=2} & =f(2){g}^{′}(2)+{f}^{′}(2)g(2) \\  & =18\cdot 4+12\cdot 6 \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$

q-166146.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=-2$ directly into the limit, we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{3f(x)-g(x)}{x+2} & ={\frac{3f(x)-g(x)}{x+2}|}_{x=-2} \\  & =\frac{3f(-2)-g(-2)}{-2+2} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2-6}{0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{3f(x)-g(x)}{x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{{(3f(x)-g(x))}^{′}}{{(x+2)}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,-2}[3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $x=-2$ again, and this time, we are able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-2}[3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)] & ={[3{f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x)]|}_{x=-2} \\  & =3{f}^{′}(-2)-{g}^{′}(-2) \\  & =3\cdot 12-(-4) \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,-2}\frac{3f(x)-g(x)}{x+2}=40.$

q-166147.worked_solution:
Notice that $g(x)$ is continuous on the interval $[-4,-1]$ and differentiable on  $(-4,-1).$

Given that $g(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, the mean value theorem states the following: 

*There exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that*

$$
{g}^{′}(c)=\frac{g(b)-g(a)}{b-a}.
$$

In our case, we have $a=-4$ and $b=-1.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(c) & =\frac{g(-1)-g(-4)}{-1-(-4)} \\  & =\frac{1-(-1)}{-1+4} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

 *The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $c\in (-4,-1)$ such that ${g}^{′}(c)=\frac{2}{3}.$*

There exists a point c∈(a,b) such that g′(c)=g(b)−g(a)b−a.

We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{f}^{′}(x)≈\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=2.1.$ 

We choose the step size $h>0$ to be as small as possible. In this case, $h=0.1$ since the nearest backward point, for which we know the value of $f(x),$ is $f(2)=18$ (from the table above).

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2.1) & ≈\frac{f(2.1)-f(2.1-0.1)}{0.1} \\  & =10(f(2.1)-f(2)) \\  & =10(21-18) \\  & =10\cdot 3 \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we differentiate $x=\frac{3}{5y-2}$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{3}{5y-2}) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}((5y-2)^{-1}) \\  & =-3(5y-2)^{-2}\cdot 5 \\  & =-\frac{15}{(5y-2)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{15}(5y-2)^{2}.
$$
